title: Acute:chronic workload ratio: conceptual issues and fundamental pitfalls
authors: Impellizzeri FM, Tenan MS, Kempton T, Novak A, Coutts AJ
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
population: Not applicable (conceptual and methodological critique of ACWR research)
findings: No studies have properly tried to estimate causal effects of ACWR, so manipulating ACWR to change injury rates remains conjecture and overinterpretation.

ACWR is the most popular training-load-based prognostic factor, but no study has properly tried to estimate causal effects, so manipulating ACWR to change injury rates remains conjecture and an overinterpretation of the data.

The authors state ACWR is an inaccurate metric (it fails to normalize the numerator by the denominator even when uncoupled), ambiguous, lacks background rationale for a causal role, and is not consistently and unidirectionally related to injury risk.

Stated conclusion: there is no evidence supporting use of ACWR in training-load-management systems or for training recommendations aimed at reducing injury risk; the ratio adds noise and creates statistical artifacts.
limitations: Critique rather than new data; absence of causal evidence is not proof of no relationship.
implications: Do not use an ACWR threshold (such as 0.8-1.3) as a safety rule or hard cap in the plan generator.
If load trend is shown, show acute and chronic load separately, and limit weekly progression with explicit conservative rules supported by other evidence.
Do not make ACWR a hard constraint or sole safety score; do not optimise the plan towards an ACWR target.
If an ACWR is displayed, show it as a descriptive metric with no 'sweet spot' claim.
Prefer simple auditable rules on absolute changes (session vs longest recent run, weekly volume change) over ratio thresholds.
Do not use an ACWR band as a hard rule for blocking or allowing load; if displayed, label it descriptive and make no injury-prediction claims.
Control ramp with simple capped week-to-week increases and scheduled recovery weeks combined with athlete-reported and efficiency signals.
Do not use an ACWR band (e.g. 0.8 to 1.3) as a hard safety gate or as the justification for progression; if shown, present it as a descriptive, low-confidence indicator.
Limit progression with explicit, stated expert-rule caps on volume and long-run increases rather than ratio thresholds claimed to prevent injury.
Do not market any load metric in the app as injury prediction.
